records.claim: EVM can be equivalently useful as signal to noise ratio and bit error rate
records.quote: We also compare among the different performance metrics and show that EVM can be equivalently useful as signal to noise ratio and bit error rate.
records.section: On The Error Vector Magnitude As A Performance Metric And Comparative Analysis

records.claim: EVM expresses the difference between the expected complex voltage of a demodulated symbol and the value of the actual received symbol.
records.quote: EVM expresses the difference between the expected complex voltage of a demodulated symbol and the value of the actual received symbol.

records.claim: Compared to BER, EVM is more of a measure of errors between the measured symbols and expected symbols.
records.quote: Compared to the bit error rate (BER), which gives a simple one-to-one binary decision as to whether a bit is erroneous or not, EVM is more of a measure of errors between the measured symbols and expected symbols.

records.claim: For BER measurement, the signal must be demodulated first at the receiver side.
records.quote: However, for BER measurement, it is incumbent that signal must be demodulated first at the receiver side.

records.claim: For adaptive systems like MBER based adaptive modulation systems, every update in the adaptive algorithm requires feedback from the receiver end for BER measurement.
records.quote: For many of today's adaptive systems, viz. minimum bit error rate (MBER) based adaptive modulation systems etc., this means that for every update in the adaptive algorithm, it has to receive feedback from the receiver end

scope_ref_ref.surface: minimum bit error rate (MBER) based adaptive modulation systems

records.claim: EVM can give the desired performance metric before the demodulation can actually takes place.
records.quote: In this paper, we show that for such systems, it is not always necessary to gather feedback from received end; rather EVM can give the desired performance metric before the demodulation can actually takes place.

records.claim: BER is a direct consequence of EVM.
records.quote: This can be done without any major change of algorithm in adaptive systems, since BER is a direct consequence of EVM.

records.claim: BER can be shown as a direct function of the EVM.
records.quote: The novelty in this paper lies in that the BER can be shown as a direct function of the EVM and as such in order to find equivalent performance metric, EVM can be often more useful.

records.claim: Pilots and training bits are always BPSK modulated.
records.quote: The fact that pilots and training bits are always BPSK modulated, it is also possible to have more than one modulation scheme within a burst

records.claim: Bit Error Rate (BER) describes the probability of error in terms of number of erroneous bits per bit transmitted.
records.quote: Bit Error Rate (BER) is a commonly used performance metric which describes the probability of error in terms of number of erroneous bits per bit transmitted.

records.claim: Traditional detection approaches rely heavily on supervised classifiers trained with extensive labeled datasets and external threshold optimization, severely limiting their interpretability, adaptability, and effectiveness in realistic zero-shot scenarios.
records.quote: Traditional detection approaches rely heavily on supervised classifiers trained with extensive labeled datasets and external threshold optimization (Jawahar et al., 2020; Bakhtin et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2023), severely limiting their interpretability, adaptability, and effectiveness in realistic zero-shot scenarios, where domain-specific calibration datasets are frequently unavailable (Bao et al., 2024; Verma et al., 2024).

records.claim: AGENT-X is a novel zero-shot multi-agent detection framework rooted in theories drawn from classical rhetoric and systemic functional linguistics.
records.quote: To address these fundamental limitations, we propose AGENT-X, a novel zero-shot multi-agent detection framework rooted in theories drawn from classical rhetoric and systemic functional linguistics (Halliday, 1978; Simpson, 2004).

records.claim: AGENT-X employs specialized LLM agents that independently analyze texts within semantic, stylistic, and structural linguistic dimensions, generating explicit classification decisions, detailed linguistic reasoning, and robustly calibrated confidence scores via semantic steering methods.
records.quote: $AGENT-X$ employs specialized LLM agents, each independently analyzing texts within their respective linguistic dimensions. These agents generate explicit classification decisions, detailed linguistic reasoning, and robustly calibrated confidence scores via semantic steering methods.

records.claim: The AGENT-X framework introduces a meta agent that integrates dimension-specific evaluations through a confidence-aware aggregation mechanism, eliminating the need for external threshold optimization and significantly enhancing interpretability and practical applicability.
records.quote: Crucially, our framework introduces a meta agent that integrates these dimension-specific evaluations through a confidence-aware aggregation mechanism, eliminating the need for external threshold optimization and significantly enhancing interpretability and practical applicability.

records.claim: AGENT-X incorporates a dynamic Mixture-of-Agent routing mechanism that selects the most relevant linguistic guidelines based on inferred textual characteristics, enabling it to robustly address varied zero-shot detection scenarios.
records.quote: This adaptive approach selects the most relevant linguistic guidelines based on inferred textual characteristics—such as topical domains and typical textual features—enabling $AGENT-X$ to robustly address varied zero-shot detection scenarios.

records.claim: Existing detection methods commonly report threshold-independent metrics such as AUROC, but their practical deployment inherently necessitates selecting thresholds to translate predicted probabilities into actionable binary decisions.

records.claim: External threshold calibration introduces variability and often leads to inconsistent and suboptimal accuracy performance in real-world applications.
records.quote: This external threshold calibration introduces variability and often leads to inconsistent and suboptimal accuracy performance in real-world applications.

records.claim: The proposed multi-agent framework inherently circumvents calibration challenges through its confidence-aware, threshold-free aggregation mechanism, substantially improving accuracy, interpretability, and real-world applicability.
records.quote: In contrast, our proposed multi-agent framework inherently circumvents these calibration challenges through its confidence-aware, threshold-free aggregation mechanism. Consequently, $AGENT-X$ substantially improves accuracy, interpretability, and real-world applicability.

records.claim: Existing detection methods frequently rely on metrics like AUROC, which require selecting optimal thresholds based on external, domain-specific calibration datasets.

records.claim: In practical scenarios, external calibration datasets are often unavailable, significantly limiting the applicability and scalability of methods relying on them.

records.claim: AUROC quantifies the probability that a randomly selected AI-generated text receives a higher predicted probability of being machine-generated compared to a randomly chosen human-written text.
records.quote: AUROC provides a comprehensive measure of detection performance across all possible thresholds, quantifying the probability that a randomly selected AI-generated text receives a higher predicted probability of being machine-generated compared to a randomly chosen human-written text.

records.claim: Recent studies highlight that generative LLMs produce inherently skewed and poorly calibrated probability distributions, limiting the utility of AUROC for prompt-based LLM classifiers.
records.quote: However, recent studies have emphasized the limitations of AUROC for evaluating prompt-based LLM classifiers, highlighting the inherently skewed and poorly calibrated probability distributions produced by generative LLMs (Giovannotti and Gammerman, 2024; Jiang et al., 2023; Yoon et al., 2025).

records.claim: Prompt-based methods typically yield discrete predictions and uncalibrated confidence scores, rendering direct AUROC comparisons with traditional discriminative classifiers intrinsically disadvantageous and potentially misleading.

records.claim: AGENT-X operationalizes classical stylistic theory to achieve robust zero-shot detection of AI-generated texts without relying on labeled datasets or external threshold tuning.
records.quote: Our proposed multi-agent framework operationalizes classical stylistic theory to achieve robust zero-shot detection of AI-generated texts without relying on labeled datasets or external threshold tuning.

records.claim: The framework consists of a router agent, guideline-specific base agents organized into semantic, stylistic, and structural dimensions, and a meta agent.
records.quote: The framework consists of three main components: a router agent for adaptive activation of guideline-specific base agents, guideline-specific base agents organized into three stylistic dimensions (semantic, stylistic, and structural), and a meta agent synthesizing these analyses into a final interpretable classification.

Inspired by this paradigm, we propose a novel LLM-based multi-agent framework that dynamically integrates specialized linguistic analyses, significantly enhancing adaptability and generalization for zero-shot AI-generated text detection.

records.claim: Proficiency self-assessment (PSA) is the ability of a robot to predict, estimate, or measure how well it can perform a task in a given context and environment.
records.quote: Proficiency self-assessment (PSA) is the ability of a robot to predict, estimate, or measure how well it can perform a task in a given context and environment.

records.claim: Task-based proficiency is determined by four factors: (1) the probability and extent to which the robot will accomplish the task, (2) within a time bound or throughout a time period, (3) given a set of environmental variations, and (4) relative to contextual standards.
records.quote: the extent to which a given robot, and its sensors, actuators, and computational resources, is proficient at a task is determined by four factors: (1) the probability and extent to which the robot will accomplish the task (i.e. , achieve the task goal or set of task goals), (2) within a time bound or throughout a time period, (3) given a set of environmental variations, and (4) relative to contextual standards.

records.claim: Proficiency assessment is the ability to accurately make assertions about a robot's proficiency given the task, the context, and the robot's observations about and behaviors within the world, relative to contextual proficiency standards.
records.quote: Proficiency assessment is the ability to accurately make assertions about a robot's proficiency given the task, the context, and the robot's observations about and behaviors within the world, relative to contextual proficiency standards.

records.claim: Assessment can be performed at multiple temporal phases: a priori (before the task is executed), in situ (while the robot is performing its task or mission), or post hoc (after the mission terminates).
records.quote: Assessment can be performed at multiple temporal phases: a priori (before the task is executed), in situ (while the robot is performing its task or mission), or post hoc (after the mission terminates).

records.claim: A priori assessment enables performance predictions; in situ assessment enables adaptation to changes or transformation to new goals or operational envelopes; and post hoc assessment leads to evaluations that can inform future behaviors and longer-term learning.
records.quote: A priori assessment enables performance predictions; in situ assessment enables adaptation to changes or transformation to new goals or operational envelopes [4, 9, 69]; and post hoc assessment leads to evaluations that can inform future behaviors and longer-term learning.

records.claim: The metrics in this article apply not only to human-robot dyads but also to teams with multiple human or artificial partners.
records.quote: While the rhetorical framing of a team composed of a single human and single robot is used, the metrics in this article apply not only to human-robot dyads but also to teams with multiple human or artificial partners.

records.claim: Hoffman et al. identify three purposes of XAI: 'How does [the AI] work?', 'What mistakes can [the AI] make?', and 'Why did [the AI] just do that?'

records.claim: XAI emphasizes causal factors that a human can use to calibrate trust in and reliance on decisions made by an AI algorithm.
records.quote: XAI emphasizes causal factors that a human can use to calibrate trust in and reliance on decisions made by an AI algorithm.

records.claim: Neither XAI nor proficiency self-assessment is a subset of the other.
records.quote: The overlap between proficiency self-assessment and XAI would include intersecting sets, but neither XAI nor proficiency self-assessment is a subset of the other.

records.claim: Explanations of 'Why did the AI just do that?' emphasize post hoc evaluation and may de-emphasize a priori and in situ assertions about likely success.
records.quote: Furthermore, explanations of "Why did the AI just do that?" emphasize post hoc evaluation and may de-emphasize a priori and in situ assertions about likely success.

records.claim: Proficiency self-assessment can be used by an agent to autonomously initiate a change in goals or behaviors, supporting mixed initiative interactions outside the scope of XAI.
records.quote: Finally, proficiency self-assessment can be used by an agent to autonomously initiate a change in goals or behaviors, thus supporting mixed initiative interactions that tend to be outside the scope of XAI.

records.claim: Humans can generate text with the assistance of AI, such as revising AI translation (post-editing) or writing with AI suggestions.
records.quote: Beyond being data providers and evaluators, humans can generate text with the assistance of AI. For example, humans can revise AI translation (i.e., "post-editing") (Green et al., 2013) or write with AI suggestions (Clark et al., 2018).

records.claim: The understanding of possible human-AI interactions and how to design for them in summarization is incomplete.

records.claim: A systematic literature review of 70 papers involving AI-assisted text generation systems was conducted to develop a taxonomy of five different human-AI interactions.
records.quote: In Study 1, we conducted a systematic literature review of 70 papers that involve AI-assisted text generation systems and developed a taxonomy of five different human-AI interactions (Figure 1), including distinct human actions, controls, workflows, and interface features.

records.claim: Interviews with 16 users using prototype interfaces were conducted to explore human experience with five interactions in text summarization, identifying user needs regarding efficiency, control, and trust.
records.quote: In Study 2, to explore human experience with these five interactions in the specific context of text summarization, we conducted interviews with 16 users using prototype interfaces that we developed and identified varied user needs regarding efficiency, control, and trust, informing design considerations for AI-assisted text summarization and generation systems.

records.claim: This work provides the first known systematic literature review that provides a taxonomy of human-AI interactions for text generation.
records.quote: This work contributes: 1) the first known systematic literature review that provides a taxonomy of human-AI interactions for text generation, 2) an interview user study to understand user experience and needs in each interaction, and 3) an outline of the design space for AI-assisted text summarization and broader text generation systems.

records.claim: Formative work is crucial for understanding user wants and needs without biasing them by existing implementations, allowing future researchers to design and evaluate new systems.
records.quote: Such formative work is crucial for understanding what users might want and need from systems without biasing them by existing implementations—future researchers can use these findings to design and evaluate new human-AI text summarization systems.

records.quote: The specific keywords we used to query the papers include: 1) A word or phrase about AI: AI OR "artificial intelligence" OR machine OR model; 2) A word or phrase related to human-AI collaboration: collaborate OR interact OR assist OR co-author OR co-write OR co-work OR in-the-loop OR co-create OR "human feedback" OR "human-centered"; and 3) A word or phrase about the task: "text summarization" OR "document summarization" OR "article summarization" OR "text generation" OR "document generation" OR "article generation" OR "caption generation" OR "machine translation" OR "style transfer".
records.section: A.1 Study 1 Method Details: Data Collection, Inclusion Criteria, and Manual Coding Procedures

records.value: 1. Directly contribute to text-to-text generation tasks (exclude image/video caption, speech recognition, speech-based MT). 2. Contribute interface, workflow, or user study involving human-AI collaboration (exclude surveys). 3. Exclude papers where only collaboration is human evaluation of final results or human generating training data.
records.quote: First, the paper needed to directly contribute to the problem space of text-to-text generation tasks. Papers about image/video caption generation, speech recognition, and speech-based machine translation were excluded. Second, the paper had to contribute an interface, workflow, or user study that involve human-AI collaboration. For this reason, survey papers were excluded. In addition, because our goal was to identify types of human-AI collaboration that were not obvious previously, we intentionally excluded papers that in which the only human-AI collaboration is human evaluation for model generated final results or human generating training data.

records.claim: The time window $t$ is defined as $t = w + TTR$, where $w$ accounts for failure detection delays and $TTR$ is the time required to download a number of fragments sufficient to recover the original data.
records.quote: Definition 2. The time window $t$ is defined as $t = w + TTR$ , where $w$ accounts for failure detection delays and $TTR$ is the time required to download a number of fragments sufficient to recover the original data.

records.claim: Optimal erasure codes are often costly when n is large, with practical solutions usually having quadratic encoding and decoding complexity.
records.quote: Note that optimal codes are often costly when $n$ is large: practical solutions usually have quadratic encoding and decoding complexity.

records.claim: Reed-Solomon (RS) codes are the most widely used among optimal techniques.
records.quote: Among the optimal techniques, Reed-Solomon (RS) codes are the most widely used.

records.claim: The lack of flexibility in RS codes poses a fundamental challenge to using them as a base for the redundancy mechanism because the coding rate must be computed offline.
records.quote: First, the coding rate must be computed offline, which poses a fundamental challenge to use them as a base for our redundancy mechanism.

records.claim: Any change in the redundancy level resulting from system dynamics entails a complete re-initialization of the encoder in RS codes.

setup: change in the redundancy level resulting from system dynamics

records.quote: Furthermore, any change in the redundancy level resulting from system dynamics, entails a complete re-initialization of the encoder

records.claim: In RS codes, the data owner must maintain metadata information concerning which remote peer stores which encoded fragment because each RS encoded fragment is unique.
records.quote: Since each RS encoded fragment is unique, the entity in charge of data maintenance (the data owner in our case) must maintain metadata information concerning which remote peer store which encoded fragment.

records.claim: The problem of achieving an on-line determined redundancy level can be addressed by parametrizing the encoder with an 'overshooting' coding rate, turning a (k,n) RS-code into a (k,n') RS-code with n' > n.
records.quote: The encoder can be parametrized by "overshooting" the coding rate: as such a $(k,n)$ RS-code becomes a $(k,n')$ RS-code with $n' > n$ .

records.claim: The price to pay for using a large n' to allow adaptive redundancy injection is a substantial bookkeeping effort to store metadata information about available encoded fragments.
records.quote: Assuming that a value of $n'$ large enough can be found, the price to pay is a substantial bookkeeping effort to store metadata information about which encoded fragments are available in the system.

records.claim: Breaking the backup object into several coding blocks allows encoding separately and tuning redundancy independently, which is convenient when a certain encoded portion has low redundancy.

setup: a certain encoded portion of the backup object has low redundancy

records.quote: This approach is convenient when a certain encoded portion of the backup object has low redundancy. In this case, only the blocks associated to that portion of data will be considered for the generation of the new encoded fragments, resulting in an improvement of coding speed

records.claim: The approach of breaking backup objects into several coding blocks is prone to burst loss, which could make the recovery phase fail.
records.quote: As a consequence, this approach is prone to burst loss – that is, the loss of several fragments belonging to the same encoding block – which could make the recovery phase to fail.

records.claim: Block interleaving addresses the burst loss problem by defining two levels of granularity to partition backup data, allowing RS coding scheme parameters to be independent of the size of a backup object.
records.quote: Moreover, with block interleaving, the parameters that govern the RS coding scheme can be independent of the size of a backup object.

records.claim: Using RS blocks of different sizes to minimize padding in interleaving techniques results in different erasure protection capabilities for different segments of the backup object.

records.quote: Unfortunately this means that the erasure protection capability will be different for different segments of the backup object.

records.claim: A common problem of using interleaving techniques is memory consumption, as received fragments have to be processed all together, increasing processing time and memory requirements.
records.quote: Another common problem of using interleaving techniques is the memory consumption. This means that the received fragments have to be processed all together, thus increasing the processing time and the memory requirements.

records.claim: Fountain Codes are not optimal because the number of encoded fragments necessary to recover the original data is slightly larger than the original number of fragments.
records.quote: Fountain Codes are not optimal, in the sense that the number of encoded fragments necessary to recover the original data is slightly larger than the original number of fragments.

records.claim: The loss of efficiency in Fountain Codes is acceptable due to increased computational efficiency (linear with block size) compared to RS codes (typically quadratic).
records.quote: In practice, the loss of efficiency is acceptable, if one considers the increased computational efficiency (even linear with the block size) of this family of codes with respect to RS codes (typically quadratic).

records.claim: In the proposed application, the encoder and decoder coexist in the same entity (the data owner), so fragment generation information is treated as local metadata rather than requiring complex infrastructure.
records.quote: Instead, in our application, the encoder and the decoder coexist in the same entity: the data owner. Hence, such information needs not a complex infrastructure to be set up between separate communicating parties, but can be simply treated as "metadata" information to be stored locally (and eventually backed up).

records.claim: Fountain encoded fragments are statistically interchangeable, allowing any fragment to be used for reconstruction or replaced by any new fragment, which simplifies maintenance operations.
records.quote: Fountain encoded fragments are statistically "interchangeable": any encoded fragment can be used to reconstruct the original data and any encoded fragment can be replaced by any newly generated encoded fragments. As a consequence, also maintenance operations are simplified as peers need not track of the exact encoded fragment to replace.

records.claim: Unlike RS codes, the block size for Fountain Codes is not mathematically constrained.
records.quote: Another appealing characteristic of Fountain Codes is that, unlike RS codes, the block size is not mathematically constrained.

records.claim: The definition of block size is a tradeoff between coding inefficiency (suggesting large blocks) and the number of operations required for encoding or decoding (suggesting shorter blocks).
records.quote: While these codes allow maximum flexibility, the definition of the block size is a tradeoff between the coding inefficiency (which suggests to use large blocks) and the number of operations required for either encoding or decoding (even if linear-time implementations exist, memory and delay considerations suggest to use shorter blocks).

records.claim: The data object should be partitioned into several blocks whose size depends on coding complexity, inefficiency, and user data generation rate.
records.quote: We argue that the data object should be partitioned in several blocks whose size should depend not only on coding complexity and inefficiency, but also on the user data generation rate.

records.claim: The sliding-windowing approach virtually increases the encoding block by allowing the overlap of two or more subsequent coding blocks, which can increase performance while maintaining shorter block size.
records.quote: One of the coding strategies that can increase the performance of the code whilst maintaining shorter block size is the sliding-windowing approach [16], [17]. This approach virtually increases the encoding block by allowing the overlap of two or more subsequent coding blocks (referred as "windows").

records.claim: The typical drawback of using the sliding-windowing approach is an increase in decoding delay and memory consumption.
records.quote: The typical drawback of using the sliding-windowing approach is an increase in the decoding delay and memory consumption.

records.claim: The mode of operation that considers all valid releases as possible dependencies results in data that is an overapproximation of reality.
records.quote: Therefore, this mode of operation results in data that is an overapproximation $(\mathbb{M}_{>})$ of reality.

records.claim: The mode of operation that selects the most recent release of the target library yields an underapproximation of reality.
records.quote: This mode of operation yields an underapproximation $(\mathbb{M}_{<})$of reality.

records.claim: The underapproximation mode ($\mathbb{M}_{<}$) yields data that is intuitively closer to reality because package managers always select one target per dependency and only deviate from the most recent release in rare cases of version conflicts.
records.quote: However, since package managers always select one target per dependency, and only deviate from the most recent release in the rare case of version conflicts, we consider $\mathbb{M}_{<}$ to yield data that is intuitively closer to reality.
